result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_pairwise_similarity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate pairwise similarity between nodes based on neighborhoods. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L11313-L11448){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_pairwise_similarity( nodes=None, method="jaccard", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Pairwise similarity matrix](/assets/graphs/get-pairwise-similarity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Four requested nodes B, C, D, and E are outlined in the accent color. A 4 by 4 table gives their Jaccard similarities, with 1 on the diagonal; the B, E cells read 0.4 and C, D is the most similar pair at 0.67." width="100%"} Computes structural similarity using various metrics that compare the neighborhoods (adjacent nodes) of node pairs. Returns a similarity matrix where higher values indicate more similar neighborhood structures. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of node IDs (integers) or labels (strings) to compute similarities for. Can mix IDs and labels in the same list. If `None` or empty, computes for all nodes in the graph. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["jaccard"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Similarity metric to use. Options are: (1) `"jaccard"` for the Jaccard coefficient (intersection over union), (2) `"dice"` for the Dice coefficient (2× intersection over sum of sizes), (3) `"invlogweighted"` as inverse log-weighted (Adamic-Adar index), and (4) `"cosine"` which uses Cosine similarity. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Similarity matrix where entry (i,j) is the similarity between nodes[i] and nodes[j]. Diagonal entries are always `1.0`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node ID or label is not found, or if method is invalid. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The `method=` argument picks between four neighborhood-overlap similarities. All of them are symmetric, and all live in $[0, 1]$ except for the inverse-log-weighted variant, which is unbounded above. *Jaccard* is the plain $J(u, v) = \dfrac{|N(u) \cap N(v)|}{|N(u) \cup N(v)|}$: cheap and the workhorse baseline for structural similarity. *Dice* uses $D(u, v) = \dfrac{2\,|N(u) \cap N(v)|}{|N(u)| + |N(v)|}$, giving common neighbors twice the weight and always sitting at least as high as Jaccard on the same graph. *Inverse log-weighted*, better known as Adamic-Adar, is $\sum_{w \in N(u) \cap N(v)} \dfrac{1}{\log |N(w)|}$: rare neighbors carry more signal than popular hubs, which is why it dominates so many link-prediction benchmarks. *Cosine* interprets neighborhoods as $0/1$ vectors and returns $\dfrac{|N(u) \cap N(v)|}{\sqrt{|N(u)| \cdot |N(v)|}}$, the angle-based analogue of Jaccard. The output is a full square matrix, so the diagonal is always $1.0$ regardless of method (a node is trivially similar to itself). Beyond link prediction, the same matrix feeds naturally into recommendation ranking, community-detection heuristics that cluster on similarity, and network-embedding pipelines that consume similarity-based features. ## Examples {.doc-examples} **Comparing Similarity Metrics** "A" and "B" here connect to exactly the same two nodes, so every metric agrees they're maximally similar, even though the metrics are computed differently: ::: {#cf811fa1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for name in ["A", "B", "X", "Y"]: g.add_node(label=name) g.add_edge(source="A", target="X") g.add_edge(source="A", target="Y") g.add_edge(source="B", target="X") g.add_edge(source="B", target="Y") [ g.get_pairwise_similarity(["A", "B"], method=m)[0][1] for m in ["jaccard", "dice", "cosine"] ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] ``` ::: ::: IDs and labels can be mixed freely in the `nodes=` list: ::: {#f50cffc8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.get_pairwise_similarity([1, "B"], method="jaccard") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]] ``` ::: ::: **Link Prediction with Inverse Log-Weighted** P1 and P2 are only connected through a high-degree hub, so `invlogweighted` (Adamic-Adar) rates them as less similar than Jaccard would, since it discounts neighbors that are shared with many other nodes: ::: {#937d758c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for name in ["P1", "P2", "Hub", "P3", "P4"]: g.add_node(label=name) g.add_edge(source="P1", target="Hub") g.add_edge(source="P2", target="Hub") g.add_edge(source="Hub", target="P3") g.add_edge(source="Hub", target="P4") g.get_pairwise_similarity(["P1", "P2"], method="invlogweighted")[0][1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.7213475204444817 ``` ::: ::: Jaccard treats the same pair as fully similar, since it doesn't account for how widely shared the common neighbor is: ::: {#a5cf7929 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.get_pairwise_similarity(["P1", "P2"], method="jaccard")[0][1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: **Similarity Within a Dense Community** Omitting `nodes=` computes the full pairwise matrix. In a small clique, every node shares most of its neighbors with every other node, so similarity is high throughout: ::: {#18fb52a4 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(5): g.add_node(label=f"C1_{i}") for i in range(5): for j in range(i + 1, 5): g.add_edge(source=f"C1_{i}", target=f"C1_{j}") g.get_pairwise_similarity(method="jaccard") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` [[1.0, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6], [0.6, 1.0, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6], [0.6, 0.6, 1.0, 0.6, 0.6], [0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 1.0, 0.6], [0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 1.0]] ``` ::: :::
